Landmarks matter, artifact is almost always loose contact or a moving patient, and the tracing only helps if it is transmitted early enough for a team to assemble. Finally, note how one pattern changed a drug decision: inferior elevation with hypotension and clear lungs is the right ventricular infarct picture, where nitroglycerin removes the preload that ventricle survives on. Flat positioning, frequent pressures, early notification, and a handoff that names the finding and the onset time are all EMT-level actions that move the 90-minute clock.

scenarios.title: Cold water: 8-year-old pulled from a pond in March
scenarios.intro: At 1610 in early March you are dispatched to a retention pond for a child who fell through thin ice. Air temperature is 38 F. On arrival, a firefighter in a rescue suit is carrying an 8-year-old boy to shore. Bystanders say he went through the ice and was under the water for somewhere between 10 and 15 minutes before rescuers reached him. The nearest hospital is 12 minutes away; a pediatric center with extracorporeal rewarming is 24 minutes away.

steps.prompt: The child is limp, gray and soaking wet. You see no chest movement. His skin is cold and rigid, and his jaw is clenched. A first responder says "he's been down way too long, he's gone."

choices.text: Check breathing and a pulse for a full 30-60 seconds while your partner prepares the bag-valve mask
choices.feedback: Correct. Severe hypothermia can slow the heart to a rate that a 10-second check misses entirely. This is the one situation where the pulse check is deliberately longer.

choices.text: Accept the responder's assessment and begin working with the family
choices.feedback: Harmful and wrong. Cold-water submersion in children has produced intact survival after downtimes far longer than this. A hypothermic patient is not dead until warm and dead.

choices.text: Check a pulse for 10 seconds, then start compressions if you feel nothing
choices.feedback: Faster than ideal here. In severe hypothermia a 10-second check can miss a slow, faint pulse, and compressing a beating cold heart can push it into fibrillation.

choices.text: Perform abdominal thrusts to clear the water from his lungs first
choices.feedback: Harmful and outdated. There is no meaningful water to expel, and thrusts cause vomiting and aspiration while delaying ventilation.

steps.prompt: After a 45-second check you find no breathing and no pulse. He is still in wet clothing on the frozen ground, and it has started to rain.

choices.text: Move him gently into the warm ambulance, cut away wet clothing, dry the chest, and begin CPR with ventilations and compressions
choices.feedback: Correct on all four counts. Stopping heat loss is treatment, gentle handling avoids triggering fibrillation, and a dry chest is required for pads.

choices.text: Start compressions on the ground and leave the wet clothing in place to save time
choices.feedback: Half right. Compressions are needed, but leaving him wet in the rain continues the heat loss that is killing him and makes defibrillation impossible.

choices.text: Have two providers lift him quickly by the arms and legs to the stretcher
choices.feedback: Harmful. A cold ventricle is irritable; rough handling has been associated with triggering ventricular fibrillation. Move him horizontally and gently.

choices.text: Apply heat packs directly to his arms and legs to warm him fast
choices.feedback: Harmful twice over. Warming the limbs drives cold acidic blood back to the core, which is afterdrop, and unwrapped packs on cold skin cause burns.

steps.prompt: CPR is in progress in the ambulance. You apply pediatric AED pads and analyze. The device advises a shock, which you deliver. The next analysis two minutes later again advises a shock, which you deliver, with no change.

choices.text: Continue CPR, continue passive and truncal rewarming, follow the AED prompts, and begin transport to the pediatric center capable of extracorporeal rewarming
choices.feedback: Correct. A cold heart frequently will not convert until it is warmer, so CPR and rewarming continue, and definitive rewarming is only available at a center that can do it.

choices.text: Stop defibrillating permanently, since two shocks have failed
choices.feedback: Wrong. Failed shocks in a cold heart are expected and are not a reason to abandon the AED sequence while rewarming continues.

choices.text: Terminate resuscitation, since he is pulseless after prolonged downtime
choices.feedback: Harmful. Hypothermia, drowning and pediatric arrest are each standard exclusions from termination rules. This patient is transported with CPR in progress.

choices.text: Transport to the closest hospital 12 minutes away to shorten scene time
choices.feedback: Defensible if he were unstable for another reason, but rewarming is the definitive treatment here, and only the pediatric center can provide it. Follow protocol and consider medical control.

steps.prompt: En route, compressions continue. Your partner asks about ventilation rate. He has no advanced airway, and there are three of you working.

choices.text: Use a 15:2 ratio with two rescuers, ventilating to visible chest rise with oxygen at 15 L/min
choices.feedback: Correct. Two-rescuer pediatric CPR is 15:2 precisely because pediatric arrest is usually hypoxic and needs more ventilation.

choices.text: Use 30:2 because that ratio applies to all ages
choices.feedback: That is the single-rescuer ratio. With two or more rescuers, a child or infant gets 15:2.

choices.text: Ventilate once every 6 seconds with continuous compressions
choices.feedback: That pattern requires an advanced airway, and even then the pediatric rate is one breath every 2-3 seconds.

choices.text: Ventilate as fast as possible since the cause was hypoxia
choices.feedback: Harmful. Hyperventilation raises chest pressure and blocks blood returning to the heart, which reduces what compressions can deliver.

steps.prompt: Nine minutes into transport, the compressor reports a change and the monitor shows an organized rhythm. You find a weak central pulse at about 50. He takes an occasional gasping breath. His skin is still cold.

choices.text: Ventilate at 1 breath every 2-3 seconds, keep the pads on, continue truncal rewarming, take a pressure every 5 minutes, and notify the receiving center
choices.feedback: Correct. He has a perfusing rhythm with inadequate breathing, so you ventilate rather than compress, and everything about re-arrest risk still applies.

choices.text: Continue compressions despite the pulse, because the rate is only 50
choices.feedback: Incorrect here. He has a palpable central pulse and a measurable blood pressure. Support the ventilation and reassess; compressions on a perfusing cold heart risk fibrillation.

choices.text: Remove the pads and stop monitoring since he has a pulse
choices.feedback: Harmful. Re-arrest is common, and a cold heart is unstable. Pads stay on and connected.

choices.text: Apply active external heat to the limbs now that he has a pulse
choices.feedback: Still wrong. Afterdrop does not stop being a risk once a pulse returns. Warm the trunk, neck, axillae and groin.

scenarios.debrief: This case stacks three special-circumstance rules on one patient, and each one overrides the reflex you would use on a warm adult. First, cold buys time: check breathing and pulse for 30-60 seconds, handle the patient like glass because a cold ventricle fibrillates from jostling, warm the trunk and not the limbs to avoid afterdrop, and never apply termination rules to hypothermia, drowning or pediatric arrest. Second, drowning is a hypoxic death: ventilation is the treatment, abdominal thrusts to expel water are never correct, spinal precautions are driven by mechanism rather than reflex, and everyone who required rescue gets transported. Third, pediatric ratios exist because children arrest from breathing failure: 15:2 with two rescuers, and one breath every 2-3 seconds when a pulse returns but breathing is inadequate. The destination decision was also a real decision. Definitive rewarming is a hospital capability, not a field one, and choosing the center that has it is part of the resuscitation.
